searches.note: Twenty seven searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's; one left unspent. Six were restricted to a house's or a body's own domain (vdp.de three times, mueller-catoir.de with vdp.de, von-buhl.de, friedrichbecker.de with weingut-friedrich-becker.de) and are read as primary through their summaries; fifteen kept the house's own domain out so that the second source would be independent. Two searches on the making of the Pechstein found nothing on it. One fetch was tried, a HEAD request to friedrichbecker.de, refused by the proxy and not retried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).
The searches went first to the open web with the house's domain kept out, for the second source of each date and person, then to the VDP and the houses' own domains for sites and methods.
Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in no source of this check and rested on one secondary source, it was cut or said with less.

The fragment's sources were changed only where an address did not match the domain the house's pages came from (von Buhl) or a page read here carried more of the record (Becker); the sources of this check are listed per change and per record under extraSources.
Sources whose title or address names a living writer, or a writer's own site, were met among the results and are cited neither in the fragment nor here.

tested: 1597: the library's year, told as the house's roots; not retested, and the Bürklin of that age stays described as the estate alone gives him.

Albert Bürklin (1844 to 1924) and the marriage of 1875 with the Wolf family: German Wikipedia, Wein.plus and the Karlsruhe city archive agree on 1875 and the dates; he entered the Reichstag in 1884 (German Wikipedia, the Karlsruhe cemetery record), so he was not yet a member at his marriage. Fixed in the story and the question.

The great nephew of 1924, Albert Bürklin (1907 to 1979): German Wikipedia gives 24 August 1907 to 2 October 1979 and the inheritance of 1924 from his childless great uncle, his father being the elder Albert's nephew; an importer and a trade profile agree. Confirmed. The eldest daughter took over in 1990 in every account, one of them from her mother, so inherited became took over.

The 1828 survey and the Kirchenstück's mark: German Wikipedia and Wein.plus give 1828 and a value of 65, no site higher; the Forster Winzerverein says 1830. 1828 stands, hedged as the estate's record.

The site: Falstaff, Riesling.de, the Forster Winzerverein and Grosse-Lage.de give about 3.7 hectares directly behind the church, walls and sandstone houses that store warmth, basalt, sandstone, limestone rubble, sandy loam and clay over a limestone bank about two metres down, a gentle slope falling towards the village. The knee high wall and the east and south east aspect were in none; fixed.

The making: Hawesko gives spontaneous fermentation and raising only in large casks for the P.C. and G.C. Rieslings, and merchants' sheets give the Doppelstück for single sites; the estate's terroir page per the author. Confirmed.
Biodynamics: Hawesko has every vineyard converted in 2005, another account conversion from 2001 complete in 2005 with Biodyvin certification in 2008. began in 2005 became by 2005.

The estate's ladder: Grapeguru and Hawesko give Gutswein, Ortswein, P.C. and G.C. on the 1828 map; start year 1990 or 1994, kept as the 1990s. Merchants list the G.C. wines also as Grosses Gewächs, which is why the question's distractor changed.
Others: Gerümpel sold as P.C. confirmed by a merchant's sheet; Pechstein G.C. and the Gaisböhl monopole not retested.

The questions: one key each; the wine question's second option could be defended (the estate's G.C. wines are its Grosses Gewächs), so it is now a Grand Cru rank set by German wine law, plainly wrong. The story question's key now says later sat in the Reichstag.
The rules: the eldest daughter, living and in people.json, stays described; no price, no score, nothing volatile; British; no dash.

changed.was: The house traces its roots in Wachenheim to 1597, and its history names a Bürklin of that age, a town clerk who became mayor of Wachenheim. The modern estate began with a marriage. In 1875 Albert Bürklin (1844 to 1924), a lawyer and member of the Reichstag, married a daughter of the Wolf family of Wachenheim, and her family's vineyards in Wachenheim, Forst, Deidesheim and Ruppertsberg came together under both names. He moved to Wachenheim and built the estate up. In 1924 it passed to a great nephew of the same name, Albert Bürklin (1907 to 1979), who by the estate's account led the rebuilding of Pfalz wine after the Second World War and added vineyards and cellars; his eldest daughter inherited in 1990. Long before, in 1828, a royal Bavarian survey had ranked the vineyards of the Pfalz for land tax, and the estate records that the Kirchenstück alone received the highest mark. In the 1990s the house made that survey the base of its own ladder, in the manner of Burgundy, printing G.C. and P.C. on its labels, and in 2005 it began to farm biodynamically. For a sommelier the Kirchenstück is the summit of that ladder: a small walled vineyard read as a Grand Cru, though German law knows no such word.

tested: Andreas Jordan (1775 to 1848): German Wikipedia gives 25 August 1775 and 21 November 1848 at Deidesheim, and two accounts that he took over at twenty after his parents' deaths (in 1795); one hotel page says he died in 1846, against all the rest. Confirmed.
1802 and the vineyard name: German Wikipedia says he was the first in the Pfalz to name a vineyard, Deidesheimer Geheu, beside the vintage, in 1802; the record's hedged credit stands.

The division of 1848 among three children, from whose shares came the Jordan, Buhl and Deinhard estates, Deinhard now von Winning: German Wikipedia, the Kaisergarten account and Meininger. Confirmed; the son kept the Deidesheim estate and the two daughters' shares became Buhl and Deinhard.

The two brothers: the GGW's biographies of both and German Wikipedia give Ludwig (1869 to 1914) and Friedrich (1872 to 1959) taking over together in 1899, Ludwig killed in 1914, and both among the founders in 1910 of the Verband Deutscher Naturweinversteigerer, from which the VDP grew. Ludwig is now named with his dates and the year 1910 added.

The book of 1907: the bibliographies read give a first edition in 1907 and a second in 1923, the latter in three volumes; the volume count of 1907 was not settled, so three volumes is cut. His lead of the Bavarian growers' association was in no source and is cut.
The cellar back to 1811: KuLaDig, the estate and a trade report of an 1811 Forster Ungeheuer sold at auction agree. Confirmed (the sale itself is left out, being a price).

The sale of 2002: German Wikipedia and Meininger give Achim Niederberger's purchase of all three Jordan estates between 2002 and 2007, von Buhl in 2005 and Deinhard in 2007, which leaves 2002 for this estate. Kept.

The Jesuitengarten: German Wikipedia gives the Jesuit college of Neustadt holding land there from 1764 and the name first recorded in 1798; the Forst village site and an estate agree on the former Jesuit owner; the soils (sandy loam, sandstone rubble, marly clay, basalt in places) agree. Confirmed.
The making: the estate's sheets per the author (part in Stückfass with the vineyard's yeasts, part in steel, on the lees); not retested.
The questions: one key each, plausible distractors; the wine explanation no longer asserts what named the Winkel site, which was not tested.
The rules: the buyer of 2002, who died in 2013, stays described; no price; British; no dash.

changed.was: By the estate's account its story begins in 1718, when a Jordan forebear founded it. Its maker was Andreas Jordan (1775 to 1848), who took it over at twenty after his parents' deaths and built a house of quality from shrinking assets. He is credited with selling, from 1802, Pfalz wine named for its village and its vineyard. He died in 1848 without a will, and his estate was divided equally among his three children; from the shares came three houses, Jordan, Buhl and Deinhard, the last of them the estate that became von Winning. Under the Bassermann-Jordan name two brothers ran the house together, the younger Friedrich von Bassermann-Jordan (1872 to 1959), who published a history of viticulture in three volumes in 1907 and led the Bavarian wine growers' association. The vaulted cellar beneath the estate keeps old vintages back to 1811. In 2002 the estate was sold to a Neustadt entrepreneur. For a sommelier the Jesuitengarten carries the Jordan inheritance in one glass: a Forst site, a house of 1718, and the habit of naming a wine for its vineyard.

changed.was: When Andreas Jordan died in 1848, his Deidesheim estate was divided among his three children, and in 1849 Franz Peter Buhl (1809 to 1862) founded this house with one of the three shares. His son, Franz Armand Buhl (1837 to 1896), inherited it and carried the name into politics: elected to the Reichstag in 1871, he sat there until 1893, and the wine law it passed in the early 1890s owed much to his initiative. The title of Reichsrat, borne by the family, stayed in the estate's name. In 1989 the estate was leased to a Japanese businessman, a lease that ran until 2013; during it, in 2005, the estate was sold to a Neustadt entrepreneur, and when the lease ended a new team took over the cellar. Forst lies at the heart of the house, and its own pages quote the old line that whoever has not been to Buhl does not know Forst Riesling. The Pechstein, its basalt shed by the Pechsteinkopf and spread from a quarry, gives a darker, smokier wine than its neighbours. A sommelier pours it beside a Kirchenstück or a Jesuitengarten to show what basalt adds to Forst.

He took the name to the Reichstag, where he sat from 1871 to 1893 and helped to shape the first German wine law of 1892, above all its ban on adulterated wine. The title of Reichsrat, borne by the family, stayed in the estate's name. In 1989 the estate was leased to a Japanese businessman, a lease that ran until 2013; during it, in 2005, the estate was sold to a Neustadt entrepreneur, and when the lease ended a new team took over the cellar. The Pechstein, its basalt shed by the Pechsteinkopf and brought from a quarry, gives a darker, smokier wine than its neighbours. A sommelier pours it beside a Kirchenstück or a Jesuitengarten to show what basalt adds to Forst.

Rieslaner: Wikipedia and Wein.plus give the crossing of Silvaner and Riesling at Veitshöchheim near Würzburg in 1921, parentage confirmed by DNA, approval for Franconia and the Pfalz in 1968, high acidity, ready noble rot, grown mostly in Franconia and the Pfalz. Confirmed; 1968 added.

The Herzog: the estate's own vineyard page gives Haardt sandstone and VDP.Erste Lage; its Auslese sheet gives cool fermentation in stainless steel and a moderate alcohol; its Trockenbeerenauslese Herzog is on its list. One account calls the Herzog a Grosse Lage; the estate's word stands.

The Bürgergarten: the estate's own news page says it presses a Grosses Gewächs only from the Breumel parcel, now named Bürgergarten Im Breumel, and puts the rest into the Erste Lage; one account names Bürgergarten and Mussbacher Eselshaut for the estate's Rieslaner Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, and a seller credits the long serving cellar master with planting Rieslaner in the Herzog. So older Rieslaners did name the Bürgergarten, and the record no longer says otherwise.
The questions: one key each; the parentage and the Huguenot family are confirmed.

The rules: the heir (died 2023), the cellar master (status not settled), the present owner and cellar master (living) are not named; no price, no score though the estate's press page quotes one; British; no dash.

changed.was: The Catoirs, a Huguenot family, have grown wine at Haardt since 1744 by the estate's account, and the estate believes they had probably worked vines in France before they came. In the years around 1900 the family manor at Haardt was enlarged in the neoclassical style. In 1968 an heir took over an estate split by inheritance and, over some forty years, brought it back into one hand; with his long serving cellar master he raised its standing. They gave as much care to Scheurebe, Muskateller and Rieslaner as to Riesling, and the wines they made were vivid and aromatic. Rieslaner was bred in Franconia in 1921 from Silvaner and Riesling; it keeps high acidity, catches noble rot readily, and is grown mainly in Franconia and the Pfalz. The estate grows it in the Herzog and bottles it as Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, a ladder of sweetness from one site. For a sommelier it answers the question that moves past Riesling: a German sweet wine from a crossing rather than from Riesling itself.
changed.now: The Catoirs, a Huguenot family, have grown wine at Haardt, on the edge of Neustadt, since 1744 by the estate's account. In 1968, as the estate tells it, an heir took over a property split by inheritance and, over some forty years, brought it back into one hand. With a cellar master who served the house from the early 1960s until the early 2000s, he raised its standing: they gave as much care to Scheurebe, Muskateller and Rieslaner as to Riesling, and the wines they made were vivid and aromatic. Rieslaner was bred in Franconia in 1921 from Silvaner and Riesling and approved for planting in the Pfalz in 1968; it keeps high acidity, catches noble rot readily, and is grown mainly in Franconia and the Pfalz. Older bottlings of the estate named other sites, the Bürgergarten among them, but its own list leads its Rieslaner from the Herzog, a site on Haardt sandstone, as Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, a ladder of sweetness from one vineyard. For a sommelier it answers the question that moves past Riesling: a German sweet wine from a crossing rather than from Riesling itself.

The border rule: the VDP lists the Kammerberg and the Sankt Paul as Grosse Lagen of the Pfalz on the French side of the Sonnenberg; Meininger reports a court dispute with the estate over the K.B. and S.P. letters on labels of wine from French ground, and another Meininger piece says EU law may call for other words for such wine. The rule as the author wrote it, with its reverse, could not be settled and is cut; the record says what is done, made at Schweigen and sold as Pfalz.

The Kammerberg: the VDP gives the Benedictine monks of Wissembourg and their Kammerweine, the site forgotten until Friedrich Becker took it up in 1965, a slope falling south towards Wissembourg at up to 30 per cent, weathered limestone, loam and clay over pure limestone, and night winds from the Lauter valley; the estate's pages give the same 1965 and soils. Confirmed; 200 to 250 metres was not on the page as read and became the gradient.

The making: the estate's own red wine pages give destemming, open fermentation in wooden vats with daily punching down, French oak barriques and up to twenty months; young barriques was not in this check's reading and is now French oak barriques.
The label: the estate's Lagen page gives KB (formerly Kammerberg); the record keeps KB and adds Pfalz.

changed.was: For generations the Beckers of Schweigen ran a mixed farm on the southern edge of the Pfalz, and after the war the village's growers founded a cooperative to set winemaking going again. In 1973 the son who took over stopped selling grapes to that cooperative and filled the first bottles under the family's own name, with a fox on the label that soon became the estate's mark. He turned to Spätburgunder, which the estate says has grown on these limestone slopes for centuries. Those slopes are the heart of the story. The vineyards between Schweigen and Wissembourg changed their nationality so often that they were called Wechsellagen, and the Schweigener Sonnenberg runs over the border into France; grapes from its French side may be sold as German wine, though not the other way round. The Kammerberg lies on that side. Benedictine monks of the abbey at Wissembourg once kept Kammerweine from it in their cellar; the site then lay forgotten until 1965, when, by the VDP's account, the Beckers took it up again. A sommelier keeps it for a favourite trap: a German Grosses Gewächs grown in France.
changed.now: Until the 1970s the Beckers of Schweigen ran a mixed farm on the southern edge of the Pfalz and sold their wine to the village cooperative. In 1973 the son who took over from his parents left the cooperative and filled the first bottles under the family's own name, with a fox from one of Aesop's fables on the label, as the estate tells it. He turned to Spätburgunder, which the estate says has grown on these limestone slopes for centuries. Those slopes are the heart of the story. The Schweigener Sonnenberg runs over the border into France, and the Kammerberg lies on its French side, facing Wissembourg, yet its wine is made at Schweigen and sold as Pfalz. Benedictine monks of the abbey at Wissembourg once kept Kammerweine from it in their cellar; the site then lay forgotten until 1965, when, by the VDP's account and the estate's, a Becker took it up again. A sommelier keeps it for a favourite trap: a German Grosses Gewächs grown in France.
changed.why: The postwar cooperative and the Wechsellagen were in no source; the legal rule and its reverse could not be settled; 1973 and the fox as the estate and two accounts give them; 1965 by the VDP and the estate.
